Chapter 8: Integrating Brevity into Daily Routines
If you really want brevity to stick, it’s got to become part of your everyday life.
Think about it—not just for big presentations or those all-important emails, but in everything you do. From team huddles and status updates, to giving feedback or just having a quick chat in the hallway, concise communication should be your go-to.
Here’s a way to picture it: Brevity is like a muscle. The more you work it, the stronger and more natural it gets.
So, how do you build that muscle day after day?
Let’s look at a few daily practices:
First, every morning, jot down your “top three”—the three most important things you need to communicate that day.
Next, use checklists for routine messages. If you’re sending updates or making requests, a simple checklist helps keep things focused and prevents you from drifting off-topic.
Here’s another trick—before you speak or type, pause for a moment. Ask yourself, “What’s my main point here?” Clarifying your idea before you start makes it so much easier to keep things brief.
And before you hit send, review and revise. Ask, “Can I make this shorter or clearer?” You’d be surprised how often the answer is yes.
In meetings, try starting off with a quick summary of the key points, and always wrap up with clear action items—so everyone knows what’s next.
When you’re writing, templates or regular formats can be a lifesaver. They keep your messages on track and help avoid unnecessary details.
Don’t forget, technology can be your ally here. Set reminders to review your drafts, use editing tools that highlight wordiness, or create shared templates with your team. These little tweaks make brevity a whole lot easier.
Now, the goal isn’t to strip away all the details. It’s about making sure every message is purposeful and clear.
Over time, these small changes add up. You’ll notice your team’s communication gets sharper, meetings run smoother, and everyone saves a little more time and energy.
That’s how you create a culture where clarity and efficiency are just the way things are done.
